topic: LTE radio: OFDMA and resource blocks
title: LTE peak rate from resource blocks
instructions:
## Where "150 Mbps" comes from

An operator advertises LTE "up to 150 Mbps" on a 20 MHz carrier. Work it out from the radio grid.

The LTE downlink uses OFDMA with **15 kHz** subcarriers. A **resource block** is 12 subcarriers wide and one 0.5 ms slot long. With the normal cyclic prefix a slot has 7 OFDM symbols, so one 1 ms subframe has 14. A resource element is one subcarrier for one symbol.

## Do this

1. The bandwidth of one resource block, in kHz.
2. A 20 MHz carrier uses 90% of its width for subcarriers. How many resource blocks fit?
3. Resource elements in one resource block over one 1 ms subframe.
4. Peak raw rate in Mbps for the whole carrier with 64-QAM (6 bits per element) and one layer.
5. The same with 2×2 MIMO (two layers).
6. About a quarter of elements carry control channels and reference signals. The rate left for data, in Mbps.

The plot shows the single-layer raw rate as a function of the number of resource blocks.
hints: 168 elements × 100 blocks × 6 bits per millisecond, then convert bits per ms to Mbps.

realityNote: The "150 Mbps" category-4 LTE figure is this calculation. Real users share the resource blocks with everyone else in the cell and rarely get 64-QAM at the cell edge, so typical speeds are a fraction of it.
